Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Explanation

Your application is trying to reach external resources via HTTP protocol.

For Managed Instance on App Service, secure connectivity to internal/on-prem HTTP services is managed via plan-level VNet integration and private endpoints. Keep inbound traffic restricted to 80/443; capture any required HTTP config in install scripts. Use Bastion JIT RDP only for diagnostics—persist all changes via install scripts. Outbound traffic does not impose similar restrictions.

While if targeting other Azure compute services, ensure the resources it is trying to reach are accessible from the Azure environment. If those HTTP requests are sent to internal services or services hosted on-prem, you probably will need to migrate those services to Azure as well.

Also, keep in mind that Azure App Service supports port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS traffic. If you are using any other ports, you need to update them before moving to Azure.

Synchronous API usage detected
 Optional 1
FilePosition
HostingPostMigrationIT.csLine 381

Explanation

Synchronous API usage detected.

Using synchronous APIs can lead to more performance issues in Azure compared to on-premises environments due to different latency profiles. Consider adopting asynchronous code patterns.

In heavily loaded systems, especially where the I/O is substantial, using asynchronous patterns can improve overall throughput and performance. Asynchronous APIs enable a small pool of threads to manage thousands of concurrent requests without waiting on blocking calls. Instead of waiting for a long-running synchronous task to finish, the thread can handle another request. Conversely, numerous synchronous blocking calls can cause thread pool starvation and degrade response times.

Refer to the links below to learn more about asynchronous programming.

Data Storage & External Services

The application stores commerce and identity data in a configured SQL Server database. Session state and System.Runtime.Caching use in-process memory. Recommendations can call a configured HTTPS scoring endpoint, account messages use SMTP, and external OAuth providers are optional; none of those external services are required for the default disabled recommendation configuration.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • One deployable web application owns MVC, API, identity, persistence, and SignalR concerns.
  • EF Core accesses SQL Server through the shared ICaldovaAssetManagerContext; focused order and raincheck query services provide selected read/write operations.
  • Recommendation and social-login integrations are configuration-gated; there is no message broker or service-discovery component.

DTOs & Contracts

The JSON API returns the Product and Raincheck domain models directly and accepts a Raincheck request body. MVC account operations use request view models such as LoginViewModel, RegisterViewModel, and ResetPasswordViewModel; checkout binds an Order. OrderDetailsViewModel and ProductViewModel are presentation response models. No gateway aggregation DTO, active OpenAPI document, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema was found. JSON is configured with System.Text.Json for MVC/SignalR, while Newtonsoft.Json is used for product details and recommendation responses.

Communication Patterns

Controllers call application services synchronously; EF Core performs database operations through the shared context. The optional recommendation integration uses an HTTPS scoring endpoint with a 30-second HttpClient timeout and no retry or circuit-breaker policy. Account email is sent synchronously through configured SMTP with TLS enabled. External sign-in uses provider middleware; there is no service discovery, API gateway, asynchronous broker, or cross-service aggregation.

Cookie authentication is provided by ASP.NET Core Identity, with authorization attributes on account management, checkout, orders and admin controllers. The JSON product and raincheck API controllers do not declare authorization attributes. Production hosting enables HTTPS redirection and HSTS; development does not enable those middleware components. Database transport security depends on the externally supplied connection string.

Core Business Workflows

Caldova Asset Manager supports an online storefront with product discovery, session-associated shopping carts, authenticated checkout, customer accounts, and store-issued rainchecks. Administrators manage catalog content and can notify connected clients about announcements.

All bounded contexts are modules in one application and share the same EF Core context and SQL Server database; no inter-service event or REST exchange exists between them.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse Catalog and Search

  1. A visitor opens the storefront or selects a category.
  2. The Store controller reads categories/products through the shared context and may serve cached product/catalog results.
  3. Search submits a query to StringContainsProductSearch, which matches normalized product titles and returns matching Products.
  4. If recommendations are enabled, the application asks the configured scoring endpoint for product identifiers and maps those identifiers to local Product records. The recommendation request has a 30-second HTTP timeout; a failed external request can propagate to the caller.

Workflow 2: Add Items and Place an Order

  1. A visitor adds a product to a cart. The application creates or updates a CartItem associated with a session-generated cart identifier.
  2. The cart page loads product details and computes subtotal, shipping, tax and total for display.
  3. An authenticated customer submits checkout details. The application assigns the username and date from the authenticated session, validates the order model, and checks the submitted promo code against the configured application constant FREE (case-insensitive).
  4. On success, the cart is converted to OrderDetail rows using current product prices, the order total is calculated, and cart rows are removed. A single EF Core SaveChangesAsync persists the order and related changes.
  5. The customer is redirected to completion; order access is checked against the signed-in username.

Workflow 3: Register and Sign In

  1. A visitor registers with an email and password, and ASP.NET Core Identity creates the account.
  2. The application sends an email confirmation message through configured SMTP.
  3. The customer confirms the account and may sign in using a password, two-factor email code, or an enabled external OAuth provider.
  4. Password reset and account-management actions use Identity’s token and password APIs.

Workflow 4: Create a Raincheck

An API caller posts a Raincheck JSON model. The raincheck query service persists it and returns its generated identifier. Read operations enrich rainchecks with associated product/category and issuing-store data; the admin screen lists those records.

Cross-Service Data Flows

The website is a single deployable service, so catalog, cart, order, account and raincheck flows exchange entities through the shared EF Core context rather than network calls. Optional recommendation composition is the only application-data exchange with another service: the scoring endpoint returns recommendation identifiers, which the website resolves to local Product records. There is no configured circuit breaker or fallback response; a failed scoring call is not converted into an empty recommendation list by the current engine.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant Customer participant MVC as "Storefront and checkout" participant Cart as "ShoppingCart" participant EF as "EF Core context" participant SQL as "SQL Server" Customer->>MVC: Add product to cart MVC->>Cart: Associate product with session cart Cart->>EF: Find or add CartItem EF->>SQL: Read and persist cart state SQL-->>EF: Cart and product data EF-->>Cart: Updated cart Customer->>MVC: Submit checkout details MVC->>MVC: Validate order, authenticated username and promo code alt Valid order and promo code MVC->>Cart: CreateOrder Cart->>EF: Add OrderDetail rows and remove CartItems MVC->>EF: SaveChangesAsync EF->>SQL: Persist order and details SQL-->>MVC: Order confirmation identifier MVC-->>Customer: Redirect to completion page else Validation or promo code fails MVC-->>Customer: Return checkout form with errors end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Product input uses required, length and range validation attributes; checkout requires customer/address fields and assigns order date and username server-side.
  • Checkout accepts the fixed FREE promo code case-insensitively; other values return a validation error.
  • Order details preserve the product price used when creating the order; the order total is the sum of quantity multiplied by unit price.
  • Cart identity is stored in the ASP.NET Core session; adding an existing product increments its count, and removing decrements it or deletes the cart row.
  • A customer may view only their own order details; admin controller access is role-authorized.
  • EF Core persists order, detail and cart cleanup in one SaveChangesAsync operation. No explicit distributed transaction or saga is present.
  • Recommendation behavior is conditional on ShowRecommendations; no retry, fallback, or compensation is configured for scoring failures.

Caching Strategy

Product details, latest product, top-selling products, and new arrivals use System.Runtime.Caching.MemoryCache.Default with approximately ten-minute expiration. ASP.NET Core session uses the in-memory distributed-cache implementation for the cart identifier. The cache and session are process-local; no Redis or other distributed provider is configured.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The single website owns all application and identity records in one SQL Server database. Controllers and query services use the shared EF context; there is no database-per-service or cross-service direct database access. The optional recommendation endpoint receives a product identifier and returns recommendation identifiers, which are joined back to locally owned products.
